q: Which reagent(s) best convert the ketone C=O into a CH<sub>2</sub> group while leaving the acetal intact?
h: Both classic C=O → CH<sub>2</sub> reductions work on this ketone. Which survives the other functional group: strongly acidic or strongly basic conditions?
w: Acetals are stable to base but hydrolyze in aqueous acid. The Wolff–Kishner reduction runs in hot KOH, so it reduces the ketone to CH2 and leaves the acetal alone: H2NNH2, KOH, heat.
x: The Clemmensen reduction uses hot concentrated HCl, which would hydrolyze the acetal to an aldehyde (and reduce it too).
NaBH<sub>4</sub> stops at the alcohol (C=O → CH–OH); it does not remove the oxygen.
H<sub>2</sub>/Pd does not reduce an ordinary aliphatic ketone to CH<sub>2</sub>; at most it slowly gives the alcohol.

q: Which sequence gives propylbenzene from benzene in good yield?
h: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with a primary halide goes through a cation-like species. What happens to a primary carbocation? How does an acylium ion avoid that?
w: Direct alkylation with 1-chloropropane rearranges (hydride shift) to give mainly isopropylbenzene. Acylation with propanoyl chloride gives propiophenone through a resonance-stabilized acylium ion that does not rearrange, and Clemmensen reduction converts the C=O to CH2: 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3 2. Zn(Hg), HCl.
x: The primary carbocation-like species rearranges to the 2° isopropyl cation, so cumene (isopropylbenzene) is the main product, and polyalkylation also occurs.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone only to the alcohol, 1-phenylpropan-1-ol, not to CH<sub>2</sub>.
Acetyl chloride adds only two carbons; Wolff–Kishner then gives ethylbenzene, not propylbenzene.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: These are Wolff–Kishner conditions. The hydrazone is only an intermediate at 200 °C; what gas is lost?
w: The Wolff–Kishner reduction forms a hydrazone, which in hot base loses N2 and is protonated by the solvent, converting C=O into CH2: propylbenzene.
x: Wolff–Kishner removes the oxygen completely; an alcohol would come from a hydride reagent such as NaBH<sub>4</sub>.
The hydrazone forms first, but at 200 °C in KOH it loses N<sub>2</sub>; it is not the final product.
No alkene forms; the carbanion left after N<sub>2</sub> loss is simply protonated by the solvent.

q: In the Wolff–Kishner reduction of acetophenone, which species forms immediately after N2 is lost?
h: The reaction runs in hot KOH. When the diazene anion R–N=N<sup>−</sup> fragments, which atom keeps the bonding pair from the C–N bond?
w: Base deprotonates the hydrazone N–H, the diazene forms, and a second deprotonation gives R–N=N−. That anion expels N2 and leaves the electron pair on carbon: the benzylic carbanion PhCH−CH3, which is protonated by the solvent to give ethylbenzene. Loss of very stable N2 drives the step.
x: A carbocation would require the carbon to lose the bonding electrons; in a basic medium the electrons stay on carbon, giving a carbanion.
Styrene is not formed; the carbanion is simply protonated by the solvent.
An azine is a side product from hydrazone + ketone condensation; it is not formed by loss of N<sub>2</sub>.

q: What is the product of this Wittig reaction?
h: A Wittig reaction swaps the carbonyl oxygen for the ylide carbon. The new C=C is exactly where the C=O was.
w: The ylide carbon (CHCH3) bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and Ph3P=O is lost. The C=C forms exactly where the C=O was, outside the ring: ethylidenecyclohexane.
x: Wittig reactions do not move the double bond to the more substituted position; that thinking applies to E1/E2 eliminations.
This puts the C=C between the two ylide-derived atoms; the new double bond must join the former carbonyl carbon to the ylide carbon.
An alcohol would come from a Grignard reagent (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr); the Wittig reaction removes the oxygen as Ph<sub>3</sub>P=O.

q: A student wants to make 1-phenylprop-1-ene (PhCH=CHCH3) by a Wittig reaction using benzaldehyde as the carbonyl partner. How should the ylide be prepared?
h: Split the C=C: the benzaldehyde provides PhCH=. What must the ylide carbon carry, and which reagent removes the proton from the phosphonium salt?
w: Disconnect PhCH=CHCH3 at the C=C: benzaldehyde supplies PhCH=, so the ylide must be Ph3P=CHCH3. Make it by SN2 of Ph3P on bromoethane (phosphonium salt), then deprotonate the carbon α to phosphorus with a strong base: 1. Ph3P + CH3CH2Br 2. BuLi.
x: Bromomethane gives Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub>, which converts benzaldehyde into styrene (PhCH=CH<sub>2</sub>), one carbon short.
1-Bromopropane gives Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and hence PhCH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, one carbon too many.
Water cannot deprotonate the phosphonium salt (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 22 or higher); a strong base such as BuLi is needed to form the ylide.

q: Which alkyl halide is the poorest choice for preparing a phosphonium salt (and then a Wittig ylide) with triphenylphosphine?
h: Ph<sub>3</sub>P reacts with the alkyl halide by S<sub>N</sub>2. Which substrate cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2?
w: Phosphonium salts form by SN2 attack of Ph3P on the alkyl halide. A tertiary halide is too hindered for SN2 (and would give no α-H on the P-bearing carbon to make an ylide anyway): 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is the poorest choice.
x: Methyl halides are the best S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates; CH<sub>3</sub>Br gives the widely used Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub>.
A primary halide reacts well with Ph<sub>3</sub>P by S<sub>N</sub>2.
Benzylic halides are excellent S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates and give stabilized benzylic ylides.

q: Which route gives methylenecyclohexane as the major product?
h: Elimination reactions favor the more substituted alkene. Which method fixes the position of the C=C regardless of stability?
w: The Wittig reaction places the C=C exactly where the C=O was, so cyclohexanone + Ph3P=CH2 gives the exocyclic, less substituted alkene: methylenecyclohexane. Every elimination route gives mainly the more stable trisubstituted 1-methylcyclohexene.
x: Acid-catalyzed E1 dehydration gives the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene, as the major product.
The Grignard step gives 1-methylcyclohexanol, whose dehydration again gives mainly the Zaitsev product, 1-methylcyclohexene.
Ethoxide is a small base, so E2 gives mainly the Zaitsev alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene; a bulky base would be needed even to favor the exocyclic isomer.

q: What is the main product of this reaction?
h: Hard, highly reactive organolithium and Grignard reagents add fastest to the most electrophilic atom, the carbonyl carbon. Which reagent class is used for 1,4-addition?
w: Organolithium reagents add directly (1,2-addition) to the carbonyl carbon of an α,β-unsaturated ketone. Workup gives the tertiary allylic alcohol 1-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol. Conjugate (1,4) addition would require a cuprate such as (CH3)2CuLi.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexanone is the 1,4-addition product expected from (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CuLi, not from CH<sub>3</sub>Li.
CH<sub>3</sub>Li does not reduce the C=C; this saturated alcohol has two more H atoms than any addition product.
No oxidation or substitution of a vinyl H occurs; the methyl adds and the C=O becomes an alcohol.

q: 4-tert-Butylcyclohexanone is reduced with NaBH4 in methanol. Which statement best describes the product?
c: Mainly trans-4-tert-butylcyclohexanol (OH equatorial), from axial attack of the small hydride
Mainly cis-4-tert-butylcyclohexanol (OH axial), from equatorial attack of the small hydride
A racemic mixture, because hydride attacks the two faces of the planar C=O equally
Equal amounts of cis and trans alcohols, because the tert-butyl group is far from the C=O
h: The tert-butyl group locks the chair. A small nucleophile like BH4− prefers the approach that avoids torsional strain with the neighboring C–H bonds. Then ask: is either product chiral?
w: The tert-butyl group is locked equatorial. Small hydride donors attack mainly from the axial direction (equatorial approach would develop torsional strain with the neighboring C2 and C6 C–H bonds), which pushes the oxygen equatorial. Equatorial OH and equatorial tert-butyl at C1/C4 are trans: mainly trans-4-tert-butylcyclohexanol (about 90:10). Bulky hydrides (L-Selectride) reverse this.
x: Equatorial attack (giving the axial-OH cis isomer) is preferred by bulky hydrides such as L-Selectride, not by small NaBH4.
Both cis and trans products have a mirror plane through C1 and C4, so they are achiral; the two faces of this C=O are not mirror images but are diastereotopic.
The locked chair makes the two faces different (axial vs equatorial approach), so the two diastereomers form in unequal amounts.

q: Enantiopure (R)-2-phenylpropanal is treated with CH3MgBr, then aqueous NH4Cl. Which statement best describes the product mixture?
c: Two diastereomers of 3-phenylbutan-2-ol, formed in unequal amounts
Two diastereomers of 3-phenylbutan-2-ol, formed in exactly equal amounts
h: The existing stereocenter is untouched. Are the two faces of this C=O enantiotopic or diastereotopic?
w: The new stereocenter (C2) forms next to an existing one (C3, which keeps its R configuration). Attack on the two faces of the C=O gives (2R,3R) and (2S,3R) products, which are diastereomers. Because the adjacent stereocenter makes the faces diastereotopic, the transition states differ in energy (Felkin–Anh/Cram selectivity): two diastereomers in unequal amounts.
x: The C3 stereocenter is not touched, so every product molecule is 3R; a racemic mixture would require the 3S enantiomers too.
The two stereocenters carry different groups (OH/CH<sub>3</sub> vs Ph/CH<sub>3</sub>), so no internal mirror plane is possible; the compound cannot be meso.
The faces are diastereotopic, so the competing transition states are diastereomeric and differ in energy; exactly equal amounts would be a coincidence.

q: Which combination, followed by aqueous acid workup, gives 2-phenylbutan-2-ol?
h: Find the carbinol carbon in the target and list its three carbon groups. One must come from the Grignard reagent; the other two must already be on the carbonyl carbon.
w: The carbinol carbon of the target carries phenyl, methyl and ethyl. Ethyl Grignard adding to acetophenone (PhCOCH3) supplies exactly those three groups: CH3CH2MgBr + acetophenone.
x: An aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol: this pair gives 1-phenylbutan-1-ol, not a tertiary alcohol.
In 1-phenylpropan-2-one the phenyl is on CH<sub>2</sub>, not on the carbonyl carbon; the product is 2-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-ol.
Benzaldehyde gives a secondary alcohol, 1-phenylpropan-1-ol.

q: 4-Hydroxybutan-2-one is treated with one equivalent of CH3MgBr, then aqueous NH4Cl. What is recovered mainly?
h: Before it can add to the C=O, the Grignard reagent meets a far faster reaction partner in the same molecule.
w: A Grignard reagent is a strong base (pKa of CH4 ≈ 50), and the alcohol O–H (pKa ≈ 16) is protonated much faster than the C=O is attacked. The single equivalent is consumed making CH4 and the magnesium alkoxide; workup returns mostly unreacted hydroxy ketone. Using a second equivalent, or protecting the OH, would allow addition.
x: This diol would form only if enough Grignard reagent were present to deprotonate the OH and add to the C=O (at least 2 equivalents).
Grignard reagents do not methylate oxygen; the methyl group ends up as CH<sub>4</sub>, not as an ether.
Grignard reagents are not hydride donors here; butane-1,3-diol would require NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

q: What is the main product when the keto ester is treated with NaBH<sub>4</sub> in methanol at 0 °C, followed by water?
h: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a mild hydride donor. Which carbonyl in this molecule is the more electrophilic?
w: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones readily but esters only very slowly, because the ester C=O is stabilized by resonance donation from the OR oxygen. The ketone is reduced and the ester survives: methyl 4-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carboxylate (as a cis/trans mixture).
x: Reducing the ester as well requires LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; NaBH<sub>4</sub> leaves esters essentially untouched at 0 °C.
This reverses the chemoselectivity: the ketone is more electrophilic than the ester and is the group NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces.
A hemiacetal-like reduced ester is not a product of NaBH<sub>4</sub>; the ester is not attacked at all.

q: Acetophenone is reduced with NaBD<sub>4</sub> in ether, and the mixture is then worked up with ordinary H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the product?
h: Track each hydrogen: one is delivered by the borohydride, the other by the workup. Which one goes to carbon?
w: The borodeuteride delivers D− to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide; H2O then supplies the proton on oxygen. The product is PhCD(OH)CH3 (racemic, since D attacks either face).
x: The deuteride goes to the electrophilic carbon, not the oxygen; the O–H proton comes from the water workup.
The workup is ordinary H<sub>2</sub>O, so the oxygen picks up H, not D.
Hydride (deuteride) attacks the carbonyl carbon, not the methyl carbon; the methyl is not electrophilic.
